sentences: Penniless English detectives, the lead detective and his partner, travel to the city's world's fair disguised as the famous detective and his doctor companion, hoping to find work.
With no money for train tickets, they stop the night train to the city on open tracks.
Surprisingly, the conductors mistake them for the famous duo, as do two shady passengers who flee their compartment.

The lead detective and his partner seize the now-empty compartment “for investigative purposes” and interrogate the neighboring passengers—two seamstress sisters, the first sister and the second sister—on their way to claim the inheritance of their wealthy, recently deceased uncle.
The detectives check into a suite at the prestigious grand hotel in the city.
In the luggage left behind by the fleeing passengers, they discover hidden compartments containing large sums of money in three currencies and encrypted plans.
A criminal couple, the female crook and the male crook, also staying at the hotel, attempt to retrieve the money and plans.
They break into the detectives’ room but find only a receipt from a costume rental shop.
They threaten to expose the lead detective and his partner as impostors unless the receipt is exchanged for the valuables.
News of “the famous detective’s” arrival spreads, and he is summoned by the police—not to be arrested, but to help solve a baffling case.
Four rare island stamps were stolen from the world's fair and replaced with forgeries.
A ransom note demanding 600,000 francs has already arrived.
The deceased uncle had suggested lending the stamps to the exhibition.
The detectives visit his estate, where the executor reports that 200,000 francs in cash are missing.
“The famous detective” deduces that the uncle orchestrated the theft, paid the criminals with the missing cash, and had forged stamps made himself.
He ran a secret counterfeiting workshop in the castle.
When he tried to back out, the gang sent him a threatening letter, and the uncle died of heart failure.
The detectives trace the gang's hideout to a city pawnshop, thanks to the threatening letter.
But upon returning to the city, they discover they are now wanted by the police.
“The famous detective” uses one of the wanted posters to infiltrate the gang, pretending he wants to join them.
Unfortunately, the male crook turns out to be the gang leader.
The lead detective and his partner are captured.
The male crook suspiciously fiddles with his pocket watch, which “the famous detective” notices.
He stages a fight and steals the watch.
The duo is locked in a coal cellar, where they barricade themselves.
The male crook discovers the theft and orders the cellar door to be rammed open.
Just in time, the first sister alerts the police, who arrive and arrest the entire gang.
The lead detective and his partner are put on trial for impersonation and fraud, accused of deceiving the police and the world's fair director.
They defend themselves by claiming they never explicitly said they were the famous detective and his doctor companion.

Moreover, they helped justice prevail: they exposed the counterfeiting ring, solved three international bank robberies, returned the stolen money, handed over the decoded plans, and recovered the stolen stamps—which are found hidden in a secret compartment of the male crook's pocket watch.
A stamp expert confirms they are genuine.
Only the charge of identity theft remains.
At that moment, the author reveals himself in the courtroom.

Amused by the entire affair, he declares that the famous detective and his doctor companion are fictional characters and retroactively grants the lead detective and his partner permission to use their names—on the condition that he may write a book about them titled after the famous detective.
The trial is dismissed to thunderous applause.
The lead detective kisses the first sister, and his partner kisses the second sister.
In 1947, the long-retired detective, aged 93, lives in a rural county farmhouse with his widowed housekeeper and her young son.
Having just returned from a trip to a foreign city, the detective starts to use a prickly ash plant he acquired there to try to improve his failing memory.
Unhappy about the doctor's fictionalisation of his last case, a published story, he hopes to write his own account, but has trouble recalling the events.

As the detective spends time with the boy, showing him how to take care of the bees in the farmhouse's apiary, he comes to appreciate the boy's curiosity and intelligence and develops a paternal liking for him.
Over time, the boy's prodding helps the detective remember the case (shown in flashbacks); he knows he must have failed somehow, as it resulted in his retirement from the detective business.

Almost 30 years earlier, after the First World War had ended and the doctor had married and left their shared lodgings, a client approached the detective to find out why his wife had become estranged from him after suffering two miscarriages.

The detective followed the wife around the capital and observed her seemingly preparing to murder her husband – forging cheques in her husband's name and cashing them, confirming the details of his will, buying poison, paying a man, and checking train schedules.
The detective, however, deduced her true intentions: to have gravestones made for her and her miscarried children (the man she paid was a stonemason) and then kill herself.
Confronting her, the detective confessed he had the same feelings of loneliness and isolation, but his intellectual pursuits sufficed for him.
The wife asked the detective if they could share the burden of their loneliness together.
The detective was tempted, but instead advised her to return to her husband.
She poured the poison on the ground, thanked the detective, and departed.
The detective later learned that the wife succeeded in killing herself by stepping in front of an oncoming train.
Blaming himself, he retired and fell into a deep depression.
The doctor briefly returns to care for him and, discovering the details of the case, rewrites the tragedy into a success.
A second series of flashbacks recounts the detective's recent trip to the eastern country, where he met a supposed admirer who had told him of the benefits of prickly ash.
In fact, the admirer brought the detective to the eastern country in order to confront him.

Years before, the admirer's father had gone to the detective's homeland on business and never returned; he had sent a letter explaining that the detective had persuaded him to remain there and forget his family in the eastern country.
To the admirer's disappointment, the detective told him bluntly that his father probably just wanted a new life for himself and that he had never met the man.
In the present, the housekeeper grows discontented with her work as the detective becomes infirm and burdensome to look after.
His closeness to her son is another source of tension, as the boy is becoming dissatisfied with his family's lowly status and increasingly distant from his barely literate mother.
The housekeeper accepts a job at a hotel in a port town, and plans to take the boy to work there as well.
The boy is unenthused by the prospect of hotel drudgery and unwilling to leave the detective, and says as much to his mother.
Later, the detective discovers the boy lying unconscious in the garden, covered in insect stings.
As the boy is rushed to hospital, the housekeeper accuses the detective of caring for nothing but himself and his bees, and prepares to burn the apiary.

The detective stops her, having realised that the culprits are actually wasps; the boy had found a nearby nest and tried to flood it in order to protect the apiary, but the wasps swarmed on him instead.
The detective and the housekeeper burn the nest together, then return to the hospital as the boy regains consciousness.
As they sit in the waiting room, the detective tells the housekeeper that he was too fearful and selfish to open himself up to the wife and to give her the comfort that she needed.
He wants her and the boy to stay in his life, and tells her that they will inherit his estate after his death.
Back home, the detective writes his first work of fiction: a letter to the admirer, telling him that his father was a brave, honourable man who worked secretly and effectively for the British Empire.

As the boy begins to teach his mother how to care for the bees, the detective emulates a tradition he saw practised in the foreign city: creating a ring of stones to serve as a place where he can recall the loved ones he has lost over the years.
The film is divided into two separate, unequal stories.
In the first and shorter of the two, in August 1887 the detective is approached by a manager, on behalf of a famous Russian ballerina, the dancer.
The dancer is about to retire, and wishes to have a child.
She proposes that the detective be the father, one who she hopes will inherit her beauty and his intellect.
The detective manages to extricate himself by claiming that the doctor is his lover, much to the doctor's embarrassment.

Back at their lodgings, the doctor confronts the detective about the reality of the ensuing rumours, and the detective only states that the doctor is "being presumptuous" by asking the detective whether he has had relationships with women.
In the main plot, a Belgian woman, the client, is fished out of the river and brought to the detective's street.
She begs the detective to find her missing engineer husband.
The resulting investigation leads to the shores of the lake.
Along the way, they encounter a group of monks and some dwarfs, and the doctor apparently sights the lake monster.

They see canaries and sulphuric acid being carried into a castle undergoing renovation, and conclude that the canaries are used to detect chlorine gas produced when the sulphuric acid is mixed with sea water.
It turns out that the detective's brother is involved in building a submersible for the navy, assisted by the engineer.
The engineer, who has developed an air pump that is vital for the success of the project.
When taken out for testing, the craft was disguised as the monster.
The dwarfs were recruited as crewmen because they took up less space and needed less air.
When they meet, the brother informs the detective that his client is actually a top German spy, the agent, sent to steal the air-pump.
The "monks" are German sailors.
The queen arrives to inspect and launch the vessel, but objects to its unsportsmanlike nature.
She orders the exasperated brother to destroy it, so he conveniently leaves it unguarded for the monks to take (rigging it to sink when it is submerged).
The agent is arrested, to be exchanged for a British spy arrested elsewhere.

In the final scene some months later, the detective receives a message from his brother, telling him that the agent had been arrested as a spy in a distant country, and subsequently executed by firing squad.
Devastated, the detective retreats to his room to seek solace in a 7% solution of cocaine.
About to leave the city for a much-needed holiday, the detective and the doctor receive a cryptic invitation.
Intrigued, the detective accepts and is met by the prime minister of a kingdom [the kingdom], who begs him to escort the prince home.
His father has been assassinated, and, as his heir, the prince is now king.
Arrangements have already been made for an airplane.
When it develops engine problems, a smaller replacement has room only for the Prince and the detective, leaving the doctor behind.
When the doctor protests, the detective suggests that he follow on a passenger ship bound for the port city.
On the voyage, the doctor reads that the airplane has crashed in the mountains and that it is unlikely that there are any survivors.
The detective, however, has an aversion to plans made by others and is aboard the ship with the prince.
He instructs the doctor to introduce the prince to the other passengers as his nephew.

Though the doctor suspects everyone, from the singer to the exercise fanatic to a secretive pair who later turn out to be archeologists, of being killers, it is not until the ship makes an unscheduled stop at another port that the real agents come aboard: the ringleader, the circus knife-thrower, and a hulking mute.
First, the knife-thrower tries to kill the detective by throwing a knife through a porthole, then the ringleader substitutes an explosive party favor, but the detective foils both attempts.

Finally, the villains succeed in kidnapping the prince when they dock at the port city, only for the detective to reveal that the "prince" was a decoy; the real prince had been posing as a steward, hidden in plain sight the whole time.
The decoy prince is later recovered unharmed.
In the opening sequence, a former federal bureau agent, the ex-agent, receives an unwelcome visit by a man, the hijacker.
In the ensuing struggle, a gunshot rings out.
Subsequently, a body is wrapped into a carpet and set alight.
The investigator works as a private detective in an American city, but faces financial ruin because she approaches her job from a more humane angle, much to the chagrin of her secretary.
Therefore, the investigator is eventually forced to sell the English country estate of her ancestor, the doctor.
She visits the old house one last time, where a lawyer hands her an envelope with detailed instructions inside.
Following those instructions, the investigator finds a hidden basement containing a primitive cryogenic capsule with a man lying inside, whom she thaws.
The man inside the capsule turns out to be her ancestor's friend and partner, the legendary detective himself.
He had received a booby-trapped gift from the brother of his old nemesis, the criminal mastermind, which infected him with the bubonic plague.
In hopes of receiving a cure somewhere in the future, the detective and the doctor had devised the desperate plan of putting the detective into suspended animation to save the detective's life.
Although she is at a loss to explain the recurrence of the plague to the doctor she seeks out, the investigator manages to administer the cure to the detective.

The detective soon finds himself in a world which has changed a lot in his absence, and lacking an alternative, he accompanies the investigator to her home country, where they are immediately drawn into a mysterious case.
Someone has ransacked the investigator's office and left a message signed by the hijacker.
Afterward, they receive a visit from the ex-agent's daughter, who asks her to investigate her father's murder and states that the message found in the investigator's office was meant for her.

The investigator and the detective (who uses one of his old aliases, an assumed name) mean to ask the federal bureau, but the higher ranks are stone-walling, and soon the detective and the investigator find themselves under the close scrutiny of a young agent.
When both begin to backtrack three of the ex-agent's former colleagues and friends, they find one of them dead.

With some aid from the young agent, the detective and the investigator finally receive the information they need: Just before their retirement from the federal bureau, the ex-agent and his colleagues were involved in a hijacking case and the simultaneous disappearance of several millions of counterfeit money.

The perpetrator in the hijacking case was the hijacker, and when the four agents were suspected of having stolen the counterfeit money, they refused a lie detector test and subsequently quit the federal bureau.

It takes the detective and the investigator not long to guess that the counterfeit money was used to pay off the hijacker, and the four federal bureau agents had kept the ransom for themselves, so the hijacker exacting revenge on his betrayers seems the most logical motive.

But the hijacker seems to stay one step ahead of them: their next candidate of the four is murdered as they try to warn him, and when the last survivor finally leads them to the cache where they have hidden the ransom money, it is already gone.
In the end, however, the detective finally deduces the truth of the scheme.
The culprit is actually the ex-agent himself; soon after he and his partners had hidden the money, he had appropriated all of it for his own.
The hijacker had been killed during their struggle, and the ex-agent decided to kill his comrades in crime before they would discover his duplicity, and then frame the hijacker for the murders.

The burglary of the investigator's office had been staged both to drive the investigator into investigating the case and to hide a bug in the office to keep tabs on the investigator and the detective's progress and beat them to his former partners.
With a cunning scheme, partially inspired by a famous political scandal, the detective manages to lure the ex-agent out of hiding and right into the arms of the federal bureau, resolving the case.
The film ends with the prospect of the investigator establishing a relationship with the young agent and the detective.
The city police department officer, the policeman (the lead actor), is an inept motorcycle cop who cannot keep his police motorcycle from falling over on its side.

He is lying on the ground, reading a copy of the collected detective stories, when his motorcycle again falls over on its side—but this time on his head, causing a cranial injury that leaves him comatose.
When he regains consciousness, the policeman has come to believe that he is actually the fictional detective, the civilian consulting detective of literary renown.
He also has acquired formidable powers of observation and deduction that he did not possess as a motorcycle officer.
The policeman adopts the habits and mode of dress (houndtooth-gray caped overcoat, and "full-bent" meerschaum smoking pipe) of the literary detective, along with a stylized British English dialect.

The social worker and psychiatrist assigned to work with the policeman is the therapist (the actress), the psychiatrist who had actually given the policeman the copy of the detective stories "canon" in the first place.
Her superior (an actor) warns that her job is at risk because of the situation.

The police lieutenant (another actor) is somewhat skeptical of what has happened to the policeman, but the therapist points out that this detective wants anonymity as much as the literary detective did.
She likewise arranges for him to move into a fittingly numbered apartment in an apartment complex located on a fittingly named street.
These strange occurrences take place at the same time of a case that has been baffling the police department: scandals that appear to involve a judge, the magistrate (a third actor).
Among these are the murder of an embezzler and a series of smoke-bombings.
The policeman manages to solve both these cases—and expose an instance of judicial corruption in the process.
The detective and the doctor are in a distant country attending a conference on the occult, when the nobleman receives a message that his wife the noblewoman has been murdered in a small village.
The detective and the doctor are about to return home when the detective receives a telegram from the noblewoman, sent before her death, asking for help as she fears for her life.
The detective decides to investigate her death.

The detective and the doctor arrive at the village and discover that the inhabitants are all convinced that the murder is the work of the legendary monster of the village, which roams the marshes around the village.
The "monster" is even later seen by the doctor, who describes it as "the mostly ghastly apparition... like a roaring furnace spitting fire in all directions".

The detective, however, is skeptical, and recognizes the noblewoman as the leading lady, a former actress, who was involved in a famous murder case several years before when the actor killed another actor in a jealous rage over her.

The actor was believed to have been killed in a prison escape two years before, but now the detective believes that the actor - a master of disguise - is living in the village, having created a new identity, perhaps several, for himself.
The detective then turns his attention to the judge, another inhabitant of the village with a connection to the case, as he passed sentence on the actor.
Despite the detective's warnings, the judge is murdered.
The detective tracks the actor down to his hideout and discovers there is a third person that the actor is preparing to kill.
While the actor is holding the detective at gunpoint, the doctor blunders in and the actor escapes, albeit before the detective can learn who the actor's final target is.
The detective learns that the third victim is to be the landlord, the local inn-keeper, formerly a prison guard.
However the landlord has gone into hiding.
The actor then kills the girl, the landlord's daughter, for not revealing her father's hideout.
The detective finds the landlord and convinces him to spring a trap for the murderer.

The detective and the doctor announce that they are returning to their home country, and the landlord comes out of hiding and lets it be known that he will be going to a church across the marsh to offer a prayer for the girl.
The actor attacks the landlord out in the marsh, only to find that it is the detective in disguise.
The two men struggle, but the actor escapes only to be killed by the landlord with the murderer's own weapon, a five-pronged garden weeder.

The doctor becomes convinced that his friend the detective, the famous private detective, is delusional—particularly in his belief that the renowned mathematician the professor is a criminal mastermind—as a result of his addiction to cocaine.
The professor visits the doctor to complain about being harassed by the detective and explains that he was the tutor of the detective and his brother until "the tragedy" happened.

When the doctor inquires about the tragedy and tells the professor that the detective never spoke about his youth, the professor is shocked and immediately leaves, unwilling to disclose any more details.

After reading an article about drug addiction by the psychoanalyst in a medical journal, the doctor enlists the aid of the detective's brother to trick the detective into traveling to the city, where he is to be treated by the psychoanalyst.

After noticing that the detective is staking out the professor's home, the detective's brother visits the professor while the detective is away and compels him to immediately travel to a certain address in the city by alluding to their previous connection.
The detective, who had ensured that the professor would leave a trail of vanilla scent, summons the doctor and the bloodhound to follow the scent.
They are able to follow the trail by cab and train to the city to what turns out is the psychoanalyst's office.

A surprised detective, who had not known the psychoanalyst beforehand, immediately deduces that he is a brilliant physician with radical theories and is convinced by the psychoanalyst to admit that he is addicted to cocaine and needs help.
The detective starts drug rehabilitation and the psychoanalyst helps him with the symptoms by using hypnosis.

After going cold turkey, the detective starts to get better but the psychoanalyst explains to the doctor that the detective's addiction cannot be fully cured until they are able to find out what led the detective to resort to drugs in the first place.
When a famous singer tries to commit suicide by jumping off a bridge, the psychoanalyst, accompanied by the detective and the doctor, visits her in the hospital.
The psychoanalyst explains that he helped her overcome her drug addiction several months ago but that she seems to have relapsed.
The detective instead deduces that she had been kidnapped and drugged against her will, had fled her captors and then, realizing that she was now again addicted to drugs, attempted suicide.
Both men admire her strength and the detective seems particularly fascinated by her.
Following clues that the singer remembered about her kidnapping, the three men follow a suspect who leads them into a trap to be trampled by horses.
They escape the trap but the detective realizes that the goal was to give someone time to kidnap the singer again.
The culprit is her lover, the baron.
The singer realizes that she is being abducted when the baron unwittingly mentions a detail about her first kidnapping.

She leaves a trail of lilies which the detective and the doctor follow to a brothel where they encounter the psychoanalyst, who got the idea to come here because he knew that the singer worked as a prostitute before.

She is not there but they find a murdered nurse from the hospital and apprehend the baron who they force to admit the truth: the baron had lost a large sum of money gambling with the dignitary, the premier of the empire.
The dignitary, who was enamored with the singer, had blackmailed the baron into kidnapping her for his harem.
After finding out that the baron, the dignitary, and the singer are on a train to the empire's capital, the three men commandeer another locomotive and follow the train.
They catch up to it and the detective duels and kills the baron, while the psychoanalyst forces the dignitary at gunpoint to set the singer free.
After they return, the detective lets the psychoanalyst hypnotize him one more time to discover the reason for his addiction.
Under hypnosis the detective recounts that the professor had an affair with his mother and his father killed her in front of him.
Shocked at the revelation, the psychoanalyst and the doctor agree not to tell the detective what they found out when he awakes.
Later, the detective leaves the doctor and takes a steamer bound for another city, where he is astonished but delighted to encounter the singer, who seems to have anticipated his actions.
At the city's museum, the detective gnome and his assistant, the doctor gnome, foil their longtime nemesis, a pie mascot, who appears to be killed when he is crushed by a dinosaur skeleton.
Meanwhile, the garden gnome families, including their two human owners, relocate from a provincial town to a neglected garden in the city.

The blue matriarch and the red patriarch appoint the boy gnome and the girl gnome as new leaders, but the relationship between the gnome couple becomes strained as the girl gnome ignores the boy gnome in her efforts to repair the garden.
While the boy gnome and the girl gnome are away from the garden, the boy gnome's friend calls him on a walkie-talkie, stating that there is a monster in their garden.
The two race back only to find everyone gone.
The detective gnome and the doctor gnome arrive and find a clue card.
The girl gnome and the boy gnome urge the duo to tell them what is going on, and the detective gnome reluctantly agrees to let them tag along.
A clue from the nemesis, whom the detective gnome believes survived their last encounter, leads them to the Chinese quarter.
They find the next clue at an emporium, and escape a group of guards whom the detective gnome had previously offended.
They arrive back at the museum, where the boy gnome suggests they look inside but the detective gnome decides to visit an art gallery instead, as it helps him think.
The boy gnome tries to convince him otherwise, but is shocked and hurt when the girl gnome sides with the detective gnome.
The couple argue and the boy gnome storms off to the museum with the doctor gnome in pursuit.
The boy gnome realises that he should not have left the girl gnome; before he can get back to her, he is kidnapped by a stone gargoyle, who apparently kills the doctor gnome.
The boy gnome is brought to the rest of the gnomes and informed they will be killed during a fireworks celebration the following evening.
Meanwhile, the detective gnome figures out the next clue is at the royal park.
He and the girl gnome disguise themselves as a squirrel to get the clue from a pug, and manage to evade the dog on a lawnmower.
The boy gnome attempts to free the gnomes, but only he and the small red gnomes are able to escape before the gargoyles arrive.

The next clue leads the girl gnome and the detective gnome to a doll shop where they meet his resentful former fiancée, who kicks them out, but allows the girl gnome back in after she distances herself from the detective gnome.
The former fiancée gives the girl gnome the clue, which leads her and the detective gnome to a gate at the old fortress.

They discover the doctor gnome, apparently the true mastermind, who reveals that he pretended to be the nemesis to get through to the detective gnome, who never showed respect or appreciation for him, and supposedly has the gnomes in custody, only to find them all missing.
The nemesis is revealed to have survived and plans to crush the gnomes by trapping them in the towers of the famous bridge, and raising the bridge during a fireworks display.
The detective gnome, the girl gnome, and the doctor gnome race to the bridge, where they reunite with the boy gnome and thwart the nemesis's plan.
The detective gnome throws himself at the nemesis, knocking them both over the bridge.
The doctor gnome narrowly saves the detective gnome with his cane grappling hook, where upon the nemesis lands in the water and helplessly floats away.
In the aftermath, the gnomes celebrate their restored garden the following spring, and the detective gnome and the doctor gnome set off on their next case, having reconciled.
A prince, the heir apparent to a large empire, was once the lover of the young woman's sister.
During their love affair, he had written some incriminating letters to her.
The young woman was given these letters for safe keeping on the deathbed of her sister.
The count, the prince's assistant, and the knight, a high British official, have been given the task of negotiating the restitution of the letters to the prince prior to his upcoming marriage.

However, the young woman is being held captive by the swindlers, a husband and wife team of crooks who realize the value of the letters and are trying to get them from the young woman in order to blackmail the prince.
Failing to secure the letters for themselves, they decide to involve the criminal mastermind in the affair.
The film unfolds as a battle of wits ensues between the criminal mastermind and the detective.
The doctor is only marginally involved until the final third.
The detective receives more assistance from an associate and a young bellboy.
